title: The First New Album in Two Decades
summary: Kerrie Bolton, Andrew Withycombe and Bart Cummings discuss reuniting to make A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, their first Hydroplane album in twenty years.
transcript:
Hydroplane was, of course, one of the names that Dean Wareham from Galaxie 500 considered before settling on Luna for his project. It being available, Hydroplane sort of, yeah, flew in and adopted it as their own.

And, of course, as Hydroplane have really staked such an important place in the local music community and internationally, welcome, we should say, to three members of the group, Kerrie Bolton, Andrew Withycombe and Bart Cummings.

Thank you so much for being here.

Hello.

Thanks for having us.

Thank you.

And I suppose by way of brief introduction, we should say that you formed in the mid-1990s, as Lauren mentioned.

There were three albums released between 1997 and 2001, before, I suppose, stepping away as a collective for, yeah, almost a quarter of a century.

And so we were thrilled when we received news from Efficient Space that there was to be a new album: A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim.

There are, of course, historical connections with the Cat's Miaow, a group that you also all were involved with.

And with Hydroplane, I suppose, establishing a bit of a unique sonic identity, replacing live drums with loops and samples — famously, a Roland Jupiter-4 synthesizer and a sampler with two seconds of memory, with which you managed to kind of, yeah, produce all manner of fascinating extended pieces.

There were lots of international connections.

DJ John Peel played you over 20 times and international labels too.

But, yeah, I suppose 25 years have almost passed since that period and we're so keen to hear what's been happening in the meantime.

It is an especially long hiatus.

We were working out that it's almost as long as the gap between the second and third season of Twin Peaks.

Oh, wow.

So, I guess when you were writing new music, did it feel like you were obliged to your past selves or was there a real freedom to redefine the band?

I tend to think that the only band we're ever going to get compared to is our younger selves.

That said, though, you've just got to go through and just not worry about what people are going to think or what they're going to say.

Yeah.

But, yeah, we're aware of our history, but we're not slaves to it.

No, absolutely.

Well, it sounds like a perfect balance then of sort of an observance of your origins, but also, as you say, like a freedom to embrace our own creative impulses.

We've been very lucky because Creative Efficient Space reissued some of your early material, 2022 and 2023, and it really brought the music back into circulation.

Did these releases play a role in deciding to get back together or was the timing sort of coincidental, would you say?

Yeah, definitely.

There was, I guess, in our lives a little bit more time, but certainly the interest allowed us to get more interested in doing, I mean, it sort of snowballed.

I didn't think we'd be doing this much.

No.

But it sort of allowed us just to get back together and do things.

I mean, there'd been a vibe for years anyway, and various sort of offers, but I think Efficient Space, you know, we liked Michael and, yeah, it just felt right.

So that's why we did the reissue, and then I guess, plus there were Cat's Miaow things happening as well, so.

We'd spent probably the best part of 18 months just in communication for the reissues: 'Oh, someone's asked us to do this.'

[Unclear audio at 00:04:17.800–00:04:18.840]

What do you think of this artwork?

Things like that.

And just from, like, being in fairly regular contact with each other about the reissues, it was like, 'What are you doing in a month’s time? Do you want to just get together and play some new music?'

You know, and we'd started, we had got together, like, prior to, just prior to any of the reissues happening, so it wasn't a case of, oh, they've become popular and let's follow up on that.

It was, yeah, we got together; it still felt good.

I mean, the, I guess the benefit, in our situation, we never really broke up.

No.

We never fell out.

There wasn't, like, anything to resolve or any hurdles in that sense.

It's life.

Yes.

Yeah, so, yeah, when we sort of did get back together, it was sort of on the quiet just in case of, like, oh, whatever we had is just well and truly gone.

But it is just the enjoyment of making music with these people that sort of is why we're doing it. That we got an album out of it that is, I think, as good as anything we've done in the past is a bonus.

You mentioned Michael Kucyk there before from Efficient Space, who's, yeah, played, I guess, a pretty significant role in the band's recent chapters.

How did you first connect with Michael?

He just contacted us.

I mean, it took him a while.

I think my spam filter was sort of… He knows lots of people we know and eventually, yeah, he got in touch, which, yeah, was quite surprising.

He described the album, or your new album, landing in his inbox as a complete surprise.

Does that sort of mean that you didn't even tell him that you were working on these new songs?

Well, we hinted, but I wanted to make sure that he liked what we were doing.

So we wanted a complete album and, because, you know, he, he'd always said, yeah, he would do, you know, anything we did.

But I wanted to make sure he liked it.

So, yeah, we sort of completely finished it and then just surprised it.

Yeah, because I think, yeah, he was surprised we had finished it.

Yeah, it was a great reaction.

That's great.

The title of the new record, A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, is a really evocative one.

We heard it was prompted by something, I think, Andrew, you found while searching through, like, newspaper archives in a library.

What drew you to that phrase?

Yeah, it was in the National Library Trove newspaper database and I did see something similar in a poem, you know, like a hundred-year-old poem.

But I stupidly didn't take a copy and I just kind of twisted it to the way that, you know, I thought it should be, you know.

Yeah, we, yeah, I like to read old newspapers, you know, they're quite inspiring sometimes.

I was listening to an interview you did recently on 4ZZZ.

Yeah, you mentioned apparently you spend a bit of time searching through the Trove database in particular.

Is that sort of casual browsing or more serious research that you're doing?

Casual and serious for work sometimes, yes.

Excellent.

And are you sort of, yeah, I don't know, looking for specific things or gliding through the archives for, like, inspiration?

Yeah, look, it varies.

Sort of inspiration, you know, you'll just search a phrase or something.

But then other times, yeah, it's more a particular, particular thing.

Absolutely.

Well, we're fascinated always to hear what, you know, is engaging your imagination.

And certainly reading through the track list, listening to the album, there's so much that's very evocative.

And when we talk about the historical archives, there's a song on the new album which is called Incident at Westall, which you might get a chance to listen to.

It refers, as we've learned, to a famous 1966 UFO sighting here in Victoria, in which I think about 200 students and teachers witnessed unidentified flying objects circling their heads and landing in nearby fields in broad daylight.

Apparently it's a mystery that's unsolved to this day, according to Australian Geographic.

So what aspect of that story most interests you and how did it find a place on the album?

[Unclear audio at 00:09:26.360–00:09:28.380]

Andrew again?

Yeah, because I'm sort of the Geezer Butler of the band and I wrote most of the lyrics.

It's just, yeah, because I'd read, I think there was an article in Good Weekend where some people, you know, they're in their, they must have been in their late 60s, 70s, just reflecting on that and how they thought there was a girl who went crazy and never came back, you know, and things like that.

I'd never, until I'd read that, I'd never heard of it and I just thought it was a really interesting story.

You know, sort of thinking about how we remember these things because I'd never heard of it but obviously they had been there.

But I mean, their memory of it, yeah, just how does that, you know, how does that fit with what happened and, you know, it's, yeah, it's just a cool story.

Absolutely.

Well, the album is filled with interesting stories, beautiful and engaging themes.

Maybe, Kerrie, if we could talk to you a little bit about your relationship with some of the ideas that are being explored on the album.

In the press material, there is listed human cruelty, flight, adventure, space travel.

Maybe on a personal level, how are you connecting with these different ideas and do you see a sort of a thread running through the record?

So, sort of.

[Unclear audio at 00:10:56.020–00:11:00.580]

Yeah, when they give me the songs to learn, I try and make it personal and I do my research too and ask what they're about.

Yeah, Andrew, did you have a thread for this, or…?

Not really.

Or news stories.

It's memory but I think, like, things like The Loneliest Astronaut is really an allegory of, you know, human cruelty, what's going on now.

Without getting too political, you know, I don't want to offend people, but I was definitely thinking of things that are happening, whether it's Sudan or Gaza. Even though the song is about animals in space, you know, it's more than that, you know.

So, and then there's some songs that are definitely about us and then others are just about, you know, recent past.

Let's talk about, I guess, the sound of the record.

You've talked about creating all the sounds of the album yourselves as well.

Can you tell us more about this process and sort of unspecified electronic devices that you're using?

Are you going to talk about that?

Only, Andrew likes rules and one of the rules for this one was that we're only going to sample ourselves or the samples were only going to be of ourselves.

So, there's lots of things that are looped, et cetera, but they're just noises and pieces of music that we've created internally.

I tend to, when I'm at home and I'm mucking around and making the noise, go, this sounds cool, I'll just film it on my phone.

I'll just whack that up as an Instagram story and then invariably a few weeks later, Andrew will send me a song which he's sampled something from, something that I've uploaded on Instagram.

In a lot of ways, we've just been relatively low tech.

We don't MIDI. Well, we loop in things. It's very much people playing sounds apart from when that's looped.

And it kind of has a retrofuturist sort of feel to it.

We're quite into a lot of 50s and 60s electronica, which, again, you hear it and then you go, oh, God, that's just a loop of tape going around and then modifying it.

It's not, there's not a lot of electronics as such.

So, I mean, that aspect is something that we've, or the way we work has been maintained from a lot of our releases.

Absolutely.

And, of course, listening to your extraordinary music, Kerrie, your voice is really such a striking centrepiece to the sound of Hydroplane and, of course, the Cat's Miaow as well.

We were fascinated and thrilled to learn about your sort of parallel career as an opera singer performing with Opera Australia and teaching voice.

Yeah, from your perspective, we'd love to know about how it is to switch between sort of operatic techniques and the singing style of Hydroplane.

Well, it's like they're the antithesis of each other.

Singing operatically, it's a very physical and very focused sound, whereas this, I can just be really delicate and light with it.

And it's sort of, I can call it musing sometimes if you're not really singing with a full voice.

Yeah, and it's quite a relief and a pleasure to be able to do that.

Singing operatically can be quite exhausting.

I guess on a technical level, it is a particularly demanding skill.

And do you find that there's a liberation in the singing approach of Hydroplane?

Yeah, absolutely.

And I've learnt to love reverb.

It's one of my favourite things.

And just hearing the effects that the guys put on singing really simply — it's just really lovely.

I enjoy it.

Excellent.

We certainly do as listeners as well.

In the early days of Hydroplane, I guess the band received kind of mixed reviews.

Did you feel like what you were doing was maybe sometimes kind of misunderstood at the time, like back in the 90s?

No comment.

I don't really think about it, to be perfectly honest.

We just did our thing.

I don't know even so much, it may have been misunderstood.

For the most part, it just seemed like it went out to a vacuum and we didn't hear anything back, good, bad or indifferent.

And, like, I remember we got a phone call saying, oh, John Peel's playing it.

And we were just like, oh, that's cool.

And that was as far as it went.

But, yeah, the weirdest thing is that now, like, we're doing things like this and that people are noticing us and people are receptive to what we're doing.

Bart's got this ongoing thing with emails headed 'Things that didn’t happen in the 90s.'

And this would fall into it. It's like, 'We're being asked to come into RRR. Okay, yeah.'

Venues contacting us, promoters contacting us, things like that just never happened.

Yeah, it's great.

It's very gratifying.

I mean, I kind of look back at the 90s, we were a bit out of time, a bit out of place.

But we're never really chasing...

No.

Maybe you were ahead of your time.

It was just about recording, really.

[Unclear audio at 00:17:23.060–00:17:28.380]

We will focus on writing and recording.

And that was, that was the focus.

That was enough.

Yeah, it wasn't, we didn't play live that much.

We just felt the best use of our time and energy was in documenting what we were doing.

Ridiculously, it has paid off 30 years down the track in that we had a back catalogue ready to be rolled out when there was an audience for it.

Absolutely.

And it's beautiful to hear that there is a growing list of things that didn't happen in the 90s that you're able to enjoy and celebrate now.

And of course, like, yeah, there is that sort of almost kind of mythological status that the band have cultivated, which is, yeah, beautiful to see you getting the chance to enjoy it.

And you did mention just there, of course, that you were never much of a live band, it was more of a studio-based project.

We did see in February this year you played at the NTS Naarm event.

How did that feel to sort of be back in the live incarnation?

And is it maybe the sort of the start of a new chapter of live performances for the group?

Oh, okay.

It's kind of lovely, really, because we have fun recording, but it can be quite separate.

It's not in the same room at the same time.

So actually playing, like we didn't miss out back in the 90s because these guys were playing in other bands and I was pursuing the opera thing.

So we were all performing, but it's really lovely to be able to do this and do it together.

It's really nice.

Absolutely.

And revisiting old songs.

Yeah.

I mean, it's...

I like it.

I'm enjoying it.

Excellent.

Playing live, for me, there are two parts.

It's like we will physically all be in the same room to do a rehearsal.

Yeah.

Which doesn't happen.

That's always fun.

That is a lot of fun.

And without fail, there'll be someone in the audience who will be in tears because they thought they'd never get to see us play live.

Oh, it's so lovely.

It really is.

Yeah.

Just something like that is very sort of quite grounding of...

It is like they've just seen a unicorn.

That is very gratifying.

And it's really nice to be able to give it to people.

Yeah.

Unwittingly, but it's really lovely.

I know, it's beautiful to hear.

[Unclear audio at 00:19:54.560–00:19:57.380]

Is it next weekend you're playing as the Cat's Miaow as well?

Yeah.

On Sunday afternoon, November 16, Cat's Miaow are playing with Mouseatouille and the Motifs at the Retreat in Sydney Road.

So, yeah, I'm really looking forward to that one.

My son's got it in his calendar as the Motifs are playing.

But, yeah, that should be a lot of fun.

We really like those bands, so it'll be good to see them and play with them.

Excellent.

Well, yeah, congratulations on the new record, 24 years in the making.

So great to finally have it here.

The new album is A Place In My Memory Is All I Have To Claim, which has come out recently via Efficient Space.

We wanted to say a very big thank you to Andrew, Kerrie and Bart from Hydroplane for, yeah, coming in and having a chat with us today.

It's been really lovely having you in.
